title: Agent evals
summary: Use repeatable tasks and explicit checks to decide whether an agent change improves useful work without breaking behavior the team already relies on.
overview: An evaluation is a task plus evidence and grading rules. A trial is one attempt; a suite collects tasks. Evaluate the model together with its harness—the instructions, tools, and execution loop that let it act. A grader can inspect produced code, stored records, or a trace of tool interactions. Repeating a task measures variation; it does not make the agent deterministic.
why: Manual spot checks work for exploration but leave a weak basis for changing models, prompts, or tools. A fluent completion message can hide an incorrect result. Turn acceptance criteria into inspectable evidence before delegating recurring engineering work.
example: Illustration: ask a coding agent to fix an empty-password authentication bug. Patch A rejects every login. It passes the new empty-password test but fails an existing valid-password test. Patch B passes both. The second patch is ready for further review, not automatically safe to release. These two cases are deliberately incomplete authentication coverage.
judgment: Make required correctness checks explicit. Use code to check concrete outcomes; use a rubric and human-calibrated model grading for subjective qualities such as explanation clarity. Do not average an authentication failure away with good prose. Passing a finite suite supports a bounded decision, not a general reliability guarantee.
next: Which recent agent-assisted change looked successful but needed correction, and what observable check would have caught it?

learning.relevance: A team adopting agents needs a shared definition of successful delegated work before expanding autonomy. Evals turn familiar acceptance tests and review habits into repeatable evidence for choosing prompts, tools, and models.
outcomes: Write a task with observable success criteria and at least one behavior that must remain unchanged.
Separate an agent failure from a broken test environment using retained evidence.
Compare two agent configurations across repeated trials without reporting only the best attempt.

workflow.before: An engineer implements a change, runs selected tests, and asks a colleague to review the patch and acceptance criteria.
workflow.after: The team saves representative tasks, runs the agent from a clean starting state, and grades each produced artifact against retained acceptance and regression checks.
workflow.human: Engineers own the task definition, grader quality, permissions, ambiguous failures, and the release decision.

walkthrough: 1. Define the task before running the agent. For the authentication example, record the starting revision, synthetic users, expected login behavior, and a time budget. Keep grader tests outside the agent’s editable submission. Include valid login, empty input, and a separate unfamiliar case for later validation.

2. Run the actual configuration being considered: model, prompt, tool definitions, permissions, and harness version. Save the patch and tool trace. Start each trial from the same clean fixture so a previous attempt cannot leave a helpful file or changed database behind.

3. Grade the artifact with trusted checks. Apply the patch and execute both the new requirement and existing behavior tests. Confirm the checks actually ran: a missing dependency or timeout is not proof the patch is wrong. An agent exhausting its agreed time budget still failed that task attempt; distinguish that from a broken evaluation environment. Inspect traces to explain failures without demanding one exact tool sequence.

4. Compare the current and proposed configurations on the same tasks and budgets. Retain every attempt, including timeouts; report passes over attempts, failure categories, and time spent. Keep a separate set of tasks out of prompt tuning. Review unexpected results before accepting a change, then add newly discovered production failures to the suite.
pitfalls: Optimizing only the new test rewards a patch that disables every login; preserve regression checks.
Reusing fixtures or cached grades can produce a false improvement; reset state and identify each run distinctly.
Letting an agent rewrite its own acceptance tests undermines the evidence; grade the submitted artifact independently.
Treating evaluation success as permission enforcement confuses measurement with access control; tool and runtime controls must enforce boundaries.

exercise.title: Catch a plausible but broken patch
steps: Choose one small historical bug in a disposable copy and write the desired outcome plus an existing behavior to preserve.
Create a deliberately bad candidate that passes only the new requirement; confirm your grader rejects it.
Run two agent configurations three times each from clean fixtures, using identical tasks and limits.
Inspect all six results with a teammate and record the decision, uncertainty, and one missing case.
success: The grader distinguishes the deliberately bad candidate from a candidate satisfying both checks.
A teammate can trace every recorded result to its artifact, configuration, and test output; three trials remain a learning exercise, not a reliability estimate.
